findings.description: The percent-decoder accepts any decoded byte except NUL and backslash. Control characters therefore survive decoding into the path, and the proxy builds the upstream request line from that decoded path whenever `proxy_pass` carries a URI. Real CR can be embedded in the upstream request line. This build's decode loop checks only `if(!c||c=='\\')`, omitting the `<32`/`127` test the sibling builds carry. One unauthenticated client request thus emits a second, attacker-controlled request to the upstream.
findings.title: CRLF survives percent-decoding into the upstream request line

findings.description: Because the injected bytes land in the upstream request line and not merely in a header, the attacker chooses the method, the target and an optional body. Against an upstream that executes commands, `GET /exec?cmd=id` runs. The injected head is echoed by the harness upstream, confirming the CRLF is really present on the wire rather than inferred from a status code. The RCE is on the upstream, not in the proxy process: the proxy never executes code, but it faithfully delivers attacker-controlled requests including an injected full request line and body. Requires the mixing configuration: `proxy_pass` enabled with a URI and an upstream that executes something.
findings.title: Smuggled request reaches a code-executing upstream route with attacker-chosen method and body

findings.description: The same missing post-decode control-character check also poisons a second, independent sink: the trailing-slash redirect. When the decoded path names an existing directory without a trailing slash, the server emits `Location: <decoded path>/`. Because the decoded path may contain CR/LF, the emitted header is torn apart and the remainder lands in the response body ahead of any subsequent response. Unlike SEC-002 this needs no proxy, no upstream and no configuration beyond the default static server; the only requirement is that a directory whose name embeds CR/LF exists (a deployment artifact, not an attacker-chosen string). A client that honours the `Content-Length: 0` on the torn first response consumes zero bytes and leaves the forged block in the stream, desynchronising the connection for the next response. Demonstrated by pipelining a second request on the same keep-alive connection: two `HTTP/1.1 ` response starts appear where the client expects one.
findings.title: Decoded CRLF also reaches the directory-301 Location header, splitting the response

findings.description: A decoded 0x20 passes the c<32 guard and produces a four-token upstream request line; a whitespace-splitting upstream executes the query.
findings.title: Space in the path defeats the `c<32` guard and splits the upstream request line

findings.description: A bare proxy_pass with no URI still rebuilds the line from the decoded path; the space still splits it and the upstream executes the query.
findings.title: Split also works with a bare `proxy_pass`, no URI needed

findings.description: upstream head split on CRLF and rebuilt field by field with no control-byte check; bare LF hides the next header in a value; strict reader sees 0 CL/1 TE, lenient sees CL+TE, or 1 vs 2 CL
findings.title: Upstream headers carrying a bare LF are relayed verbatim, giving CRLF-strict and LF-lenient parsers different header sets and framing

findings.description: any status under 200 is rejected with 502
findings.title: Interim (1xx) upstream responses are rejected as parse failures, so any upstream that emits one returns 502

findings.description: line 67 proxy(): !hasToken(conn,v.first) excludes any attacker-named header from the forwarded head; the while(body>0) loop still copies the body; upstream sees POST with no Content-Length, treats 38 payload bytes as the next request and executes GET /exec?cmd=id (uid=). Case-insensitive token match also works. Distinct from SEC-004 (RST truncation)
findings.title: A header named in the client's Connection: field is stripped from the forwarded request, so Connection: content-length sends the body without the Content-Length that frames it - a single-request body desync that executes the replay

findings.description: the whole request is refused in the accept loop; the request is refused with 417
findings.title: `Expect: 100-continue` is refused outright with 417, so every standard uploading client is rejected

findings.description: The framing gate rejects any request carrying a `Transfer-Encoding` header, so chunked uploads (curl -T) never reach the upstream. the accept-path gate rejects a non-`GET`/`HEAD` method and then any request carrying the header.
findings.title: `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` request bodies are refused with 400, so every standard chunked upload fails

findings.description: A coding-list Transfer-Encoding is not recognised, so chunk framing is forwarded as the body. the `chunk` flag is set only by exact equality with `chunked`.
findings.title: `Transfer-Encoding: gzip, chunked` corrupts the body: raw chunk framing is relayed as payload

findings.description: 204/304 are read as bodyless but the chunked flag stays set, so the head advertises a chunk stream that never arrives; http.client raises IncompleteRead.
findings.title: A bodyless upstream status is relayed with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and no terminating chunk

findings.description: number() defaults to 0 on non-digit input, so 0x26 / "38, 38" / +38 leave body=0 while the header text is copied upstream; a conformant upstream then blocks waiting for bytes that never arrive.
findings.title: Unparseable Content-Length is forwarded verbatim while the body is dropped

findings.description: SIGTERM makes the master signal workers, which leave poll() at once and close downstream sockets; an in-flight proxied response is cut at 0 bytes while toksec_drain_timeout is ignored.
findings.title: SIGTERM truncates the in-flight proxied response instead of draining to toksec_drain_timeout

findings.description: Deadline directives validate but never take effect. `toksec_header_deadline` and `toksec_write_deadline` both parse into `Config` and are then never read. Every connection instead gets a fixed 10 s `SO_RCVTIMEO`/`SO_SNDTIMEO` (line 68), so the two values are decorative: a `toksec_header_deadline=2s` deployment closes a silent client at 10.16 s, and a `toksec_write_deadline=200ms` deployment still streams 2 MB for 10.24 s. A trickling client never hits the header deadline at all because `SO_RCVTIMEO` restarts on every byte, so 40 s of 0.3 s-spaced bytes leaves the connection open past a 2 s deadline. Both directives validate cleanly, so a hardened deployment gets no warning that they do nothing. Evidence: ev_deadline_all.log.
findings.title: Both deadlines are configured and then replaced by a hardcoded 10 s socket timeout

limitations: RCE verdict is none found within the audited scope; this build has no CGI, exec, or dynamic module path, so RCE requires memory corruption
Fuzzing bounds but cannot prove the absence of all memory-safety bugs
TLS was exercised end-to-end with a self-signed RSA-2048 certificate and crafted ClientHellos; client-certificate authentication and post-handshake (TLS 1.3) message paths were not covered

Memory measurements separate real growth from ASan allocator quarantine: the ASan build's RSS climb (1,996kB over 20,000 connections) is quarantine retention, not a leak, while the production build is flat at 0kB growth after warmup; load testing was single-host and not a distributed concurrency stress
Soak and memory probes were single-host; concurrent-worker races beyond 4 forked workers and distributed load were not stressed
RCE verdict is upstream-dependent: the proxy itself executes no code, so a code-executing backend route is what turns smuggling into RCE
Requires `proxy_pass` with a URI component; with a bare `proxy_pass http://up` (no URI) the raw target is forwarded and the decoded control characters are not used
Fuzzing bounds but cannot prove absence of all memory-safety bugs
Concurrent multi-host attack traffic beyond a single-host loopback harness was not exercised
Root cause is the decode loop at line 63, which omits the control-character test its siblings carry
Truncation is timing dependent in magnitude (127,860-2,097,152 of 2,097,152 observed) but the 16 KiB threshold truncated in 3/3 on every build tested
methods: Static source review of all 71 lines, including config lexer and proxy path
21-case path-encoding probe (dot segments, encoded traversal, NUL, invalid/truncated UTF-8, long components)
decode probe: 256 single-byte percent-encoded targets plus encodings from 100 to 16000 bytes
Event-loop lifecycle stress (partial requests, backpressure, churn, pipelining, mixed readers)
22-case byte-range probe including 64-bit and overflow-shaped values
structured parser fuzzing: 3 seeds x 1000 plus 3 seeds x 2000 long-input = 9000 iterations
raw binary fuzzing with random chunk splits: 3 seeds x 500 = 1500 iterations
proxy probe through a controlled Python upstream, plus 15 malformed-upstream-response modes
TLS ClientHello probe: 32 adversarial ALPN/SNI structural cases plus 600 crafted-handshake fuzz iterations under ASan
ASan+UBSan+_GLIBCXX_DEBUG build of the frozen release, all sanitizer logs empty

Sustained-load soak and allocator-aware memory probe: 4 forked workers under nginx_mw.conf, 5,000 sequential keep-alive requests against the production build with per-request fd sampling, plus 20,000 sequential keep-alive requests against the ASan build and 20,000 new connections against both the production and ASan builds to compare RSS growth
Live malicious-upstream smuggle test: controlled upstream echoing the parsed request head
Encoded-CRLF request-line injection, two forms (header injection and injected second request)
Trailing-byte truncation sweep: 0/1024/4090/4096/8192/16384/32768/65536 bytes written after the header terminator against a 2 MiB file, three trials per row, Connection: close
